Photograph: Lionel Cironneau/AP France Gun found in French lake is analysed by 2012 Alps killings investigators British tourists reportedly discovered Luger pistol that is latest in long line of potential leads in mystery of al-Hilli deaths Patrick Daly Wed 2 Sep 2026 15.03 EDT Last modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 15.50 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Experts are examining a gun found by tourists to determine whether it might have been used to kill a British family in the French Alps 14 years ago. In what remains an unsolved murder case, Saad al-Hilli, 50, his wife, Ikbal, 47, and her mother, Suhaila al-Allaf, 74, were shot dead on a road near Annecy, a remote Alpine village in eastern France in September 2012. The couple’s two young daughters, then four and seven, survived but a passing cyclist, 45-year-old Sylvain Mollier, was also killed. The French prosecutor Marie-Céline Lawrysz confirmed that a pistol, thought to be a Luger, was uncovered on 20 August by two tourists swimming in Lake Annecy. The weapon is currently being analysed by ballistics experts in France in connection with the al-Hilli cold case. During the initial investigation, pieces from the butt of the weapon used in the killings, a vintage Luger P06-29 pistol, were found on the ground near the British-registered BMW estate car that the family had been driving at the time of the attack. The gun was identified as a model used by the Swiss army in the 1930s, but its owner has never been traced. In a statement, Lawrysz said a semi-automatic pistol had been found by the tourists, reported to be British, at a depth of about five feet, a few dozen metres away from the shore of Lake Annecy. She said: “They kept the weapon for 24 hours and conducted online research to identify its type. “They subsequently drew a link between the discovered weapon and the one believed to have been used in the Chevaline [near Annecy] killing on September 5, 2012. “On August 21 2026, they handed the weapon over to gendarmes from the local Saint-Jorioz brigade.” Detectives have so far ruled out the possibility of a contract killing, saying a professional killer would not have used such a vintage weapon as the Luger. The discovery of the pistol is the latest in a long line of leads that investigators have followed in an effort to unravel the mystery that has surrounded the four deaths. Suspects previously arrested in connection with the case include an Iraqi prisoner known as Mr S who was claimed to have said he had been offered “a large sum of money” to kill Iraqis living in the UK. Mr al-Hilli’s brother Zaid was also arrested on suspicion of murder in 2013, but was later told he would face no further action after police found there was insufficient evidence to charge him with a crime. In 2022, another suspect was questioned but released without charge. Two years ago, DNA analysis was ordered by detectives in France’s cold case unit on clothes belonging to the victims, as well as on the pieces of the gun and cigarette butts found at the scene. No arrests were made following the tests. https://www.politico.eu/article/marine-l.text: PARIS — The National Rally, the party of French far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen, fired a volunteer security official on Wednesday after body camera footage emerged showing the individual, a municipal police officer, making racist remarks. The clip, published by local daily Midi Libre , showed a group of local police officers in the southern city of Carcassonne — which the National Rally took control of during the French local elections in March — using racial and homophobic slurs and uttering a series of hateful comments about minorities, migrants and women. The individual was not named and appears blurred in photos and video. In a statement, the city said the clip was from 2025 — before Mayor Christophe Barthès took office— and that Barthès unequivocally condemned the remarks. Advertisement Advertisement “Proceedings will be initiated, and the sanctions will match the seriousness of the facts,” the statement said. The Carcassonne local police did not immediately respond to an email seeking comment. The National Rally said in a statement that the volunteer was “immediately removed” from his role and “expelled” from the party after its leadership learned of the video. The prosecutor’s office in Carcassonne told the AFP news agency it had opened an investigation on the basis of the footage. But the party’s opponents said the incident was evidence of the National Rally’s inability to fully extract itself from its racist, xenophobic and antisemitic roots. Le Pen’s father founded the party , then known as the National Front, alongside a ragtag group of political misfits and Nazi collaborators. The elder Le Pen was repeatedly convicted for hate speech, including downplaying the Holocaust. Marine Le Pen kicked her father out of the party in 2015 as part of her years-long effort to clean up its image. The National Rally today enjoys unprecedented support, and most polls show Le Pen is the current favorite in the race to replace Macron in the spring of 2027. Yet her party has frequently been forced to address offensive remarks made by lower-ranking officials and members, especially during election cycles. “This is what France would look like if it were led by the National Rally,” Gabriel Attal, the candidate for French President Emmanuel Macron’s Renaissance party wrote on X . Olivier Faure, the leader of the center-left Socialist Party who is vying for his party’s backing in the presidential race in a primary contest, said on X that voters should not give the National Rally “the keys to France.” Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck5y.text: Figure caption, âWe will fight backâ if Russia attacks, Lithuanian PM says By Tabby Wilson Published 22 September 2026, 02:04 BST Updated 7 hours ago Lithuania's prime minister has told the BBC his country has made evacuation plans in the face of threats from Russia, but added they "will not surrender" if attacked. Prime Minister Mindaugas SinkeviÄius told Newsnight that Lithuanians feel "constantly threatened" by Russia, in part because of drones entering the nation's airspace. He told Newsnight if his country was attacked, "we will fight back... we will engage". But he said there were plans for a "variety of scenarios" and used an example of getting elderly citizens out of cities "smoothly" and avoiding traffic jams. Lithuania, a Nato member, shares a land border with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. Nato is thought to have several thousand troops stationed in the Baltic state, including US and German forces. Although the US is currently reviewing its deployments in Europe, Lithuanian President Gitanas NausÄda said on Tuesday that a new US troop rotation was on its way to his country. SinkeviÄius told the BBC. "We're thinking about a variety of scenarios, not all of them are being discussed very much publicly." "We face concrete threats, not on a daily basis, but we're experiencing them and it's a true reality for us." SinkeviÄius also said the UK needed a "shift in the mindset" in terms of its approach to defence, but noted that Lithuania was "closer to the border and closer to [the] threat". Last week Nato fighter pilots shot down a drone that entered Lithuania's airspace. Lithuania has experienced numerous incidents in the past year , which it describes as "hybrid attacks" and blames on neighbouring Belarus, a close Russian ally. Late on Monday night, flights were disrupted at Lithuania's main airport in the capital Vilnius, because of what the airports operator called a "hybrid attack carried out by Belarus", involving objects that appeared to resemble the shape of balloons. The president's chief adviser, Deividas Matulionis, said on Tuesday it was unclear whether the objects were balloons. Nato said that as of December last year it had more than 5,000 troops in Lithuania, but says now that it is unable to give a precise figure for the numbers stationed there. Germany - a fellow Nato ally - has pledged to send a 5,000-strong combat-ready brigade to Lithuania permanently as a response to the changing security situation in Europe. However, Nato said on Tuesday it would reach "full operational capability" by the end of 2027. The Germany military has failed to recruit enough personnel voluntarily and is now turning to compulsory assignments to fill some positions. The majority of troops will be based in RÅ«dninkai, near the SuwaÅki Gap - a line that borders Lithuania and Poland and also links Belarus with Russia's Kaliningrad. The origins of last week's drone incident over Lithuania have not been confirmed, however Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas told Newshour that it had come from the direction of Belarus. UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said: "Thanks to the swift and professional actions of Lithuanian and Italian forces, Nato once again demonstrated our readiness to protect our airspace. "We stand united, around the clock, in defence of every inch of Nato territory." Moscow did not comment on the incident. Military drone incursions have become increasingly common across Europe since the beginning of Russia's full-scale of invasion of Ukraine. Residents in Lithuania's capital Vilnius were also forced to take shelter in May after a drone alert was triggered, briefly grounding flights and rail travel. Nato jets have scrambled multiple times to shoot down stray Ukrainian drones that have crossed into fellow Baltic countries Estonia and Latvia this year. Ukraine has blamed the stray drones on Russian electronic warfare, technology designed to change the flight paths of Ukrainian drones. Lithuania, Estonia and Latvia all joined Nato in 2004, becoming signatories to the Article 5 provision that states "an armed attack against one Nato member shall be considered an attack against all members". https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text: ‘In June, Swiss voters narrowly rejected a far-right proposal to cap the population at 10 million and terminate EU-Swiss economic agreements.’ Photograph: Stefan Wermuth/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen ‘In June, Swiss voters narrowly rejected a far-right proposal to cap the population at 10 million and terminate EU-Swiss economic agreements.’ Photograph: Stefan Wermuth/AFP/Getty Images Opinion Switzerland Switzerland’s love of referendums helps us keep the far right at bay Joseph de Weck Brexit gave direct democracy a bad name. But the Swiss approach could be what Europe needs now Mon 28 Sep 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Mon 28 Sep 2026 06.22 EDT Share F ascism rests on a two-part confidence trick. First, a leader claims to embody the will of the people. Then they argue that only by being granted sweeping powers can that be realised. Having grown up in Switzerland , I find it easy to see through this trick. That is because the policies championed by the far right rarely pass the referendum test. Dismantling publicly funded media? In March, 62% of Swiss voters rejected a far-right initiative to halve funding for the country’s public broadcaster. Corporate tax cuts? In 2017, 59% struck down such plans of the Swiss government. Immigration police hunting down migrants? Again, 59% rejected a far-right proposal to automatically deport foreign nationals convicted of crimes without judicial review. Or this week’s resounding 70% “No” vote on a far-right proposal to tighten Switzerland’s neutrality to the point that Bern would have been forced to drop sanctions on Russia over Ukraine. Switzerland is hardly a nation of progressives. Leftwing parties won just 29% of the vote in the most recent national elections . Women gained the right to vote only in 1971. The asylum law is one of Europe’s toughest. That, too, is the legacy of direct democracy. Yet, most often, the country’s tradition of putting decisions out to referendum exposes how, despite dominating social media and the press amplifying its positions, the far right thrives on imagined majorities. Direct democracy also frustrates the second part of the authoritarian project: the power grab. From Donald Trump to Giorgia Meloni , the right seeks to centralise power . Direct democracy disperses it. History shows that parliamentarians can be pressed into surrendering their prerogatives. Good luck trying to persuade millions of voters to do the same. View image in fullscreen A poster urging people to vote against the Swiss People’s party referendum titled ‘No to a Switzerland with 10 million inhabitants’, Bern, 18 May 2026. Photograph: Christian Beutler/ThirdParty/AP Enter Hannah Arendt . Having fled Nazi Germany in 1933, the philosopher and political theorist spent much of her life trying to understand why democracies abolish themselves, why the Weimar Republic failed. Part of her answer was that parliamentary democracy could drift towards the rule of party elites and bureaucracy. Autocrats exploit the feeling of loss that happens when citizens feel disenfranchised. The central question, therefore, is how to maintain the link between demos and kratos – between people and power? Arendt’s answer was citizens’ participation. She pointed to the town hall meetings of the American revolution or soviet councils of the Russian revolution as possible models. Indeed, deeper citizen involvement is one of the great unmet desires of European politics. Take the gilets jaunes movement in France in 2018. The protesters’ demands went well beyond better public services or lower taxes. At its heart was a plea to be seen and heard, embodied in the call for citizens’ referendums. A 2017 poll found that 74% of German, French and Spanish people think that public referendums would be a good way to govern their country. Yet, whenever I argue for more direct democracy abroad, there is the same reaction: curiosity from ordinary people, eye-rolling from political and economic elites. But aren’t referendums a high-risk way of governing, they ask? Brexit, anyone? There are risks. In June, Swiss voters narrowly rejected (55%) a far-right proposal to cap the population at 10 million and terminate EU-Swiss economic agreements. But unlike the Brexit referendum in the UK, a vote is never a final decision for the Swiss. Since 2000, the Swiss have voted on relations with Brussels more than a dozen times . Unlike politicians, the demos has little difficulty in admitting that yesterday’s answer may not be right for today. But wouldn’t voters, if given the chance, blow a massive hole in the budget deficit? As every parent knows, responsibility breeds responsibility. Two-thirds of Swiss voters rejected a proposal to extend annual holidays by two weeks. A tragic case of excessive responsibility. It seems that many in Europe have forgotten that we want to live in republics not only because they “deliver” in terms of rubbish collection or maximising individual freedom. Democracy’s most powerful idea is the promise of self-government: a political order that recognises we humans not merely as consumers or subjects of politics, but as the authors of our common future. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion When that promise is broken, when people feel their votes have little impact and elites always get their way, the difference between democracy and authoritarianism begins to blur. It is then that things become truly dangerous. To put a lock on the far right and breathe new life into that republican promise, we need a transfer of power from the nation state to its citizens. But here is the crux. If we really want to reestablish the primacy of democracy, the transfer of power to citizens needs to be accompanied by a transfer of power from the nation state to Europe . Let’s not fool ourselves: today, nation states often cosplay sovereignty more than they exercise it. To claw back power from Silicon Valley, Washington and Beijing, we must organise as Europeans. And this is where another of direct democracy’s secret superpowers comes in. In Switzerland, with its four linguistic communities, referendums are what create a joint public sphere and a sense of national community. In a multicultural country, being governed together is not enough. A shared identity is built above all through the experience of debating and governing together. For Europe to become a real political community, it must find a way to both connect and empower its citizens. Direct democracy delivers on both. Giving up some national sovereignty in return for more individual power is an attractive offer. It could open a new chapter in the continent’s coming together, one capable of inspiring genuine excitement. Imagine Europeans debating and voting together on such things as migration policy, the 2035 ban on new petrol and diesel cars, or taxing the big digital corporations . Utopian? Perhaps. But every democratic advance once was.
